query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 fabricated via additive manufacturing, degradation at elevated temperatures is governed by a selective, grain‐boundary‐mediated oxidation process. Specifically, under oxidizing atmospheres, Al and Ti diffuse rapidly along additive‐induced nanocrystalline regions and grain boundaries to form discontinuous or non‐adherent oxide phases (e.g., Al2O3 and TiO2), which in turn create stress concentrations and embrittlement that lead to catastrophic intergranular failure. In reducing environments, the lack of a robust passivation layer may allow destabilization of the protective element distribution and internal phase changes that similarly culminate in failure.
generation.material_initial_state: Additively manufactured alloy with a homogeneous single-phase FCC matrix, containing intrinsic defects and a refined, nanocrystalline grain structure typical of the AM process.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled high-temperature exposure experiments while systematically varying the ambient gas chemistry (switching between oxidizing atmospheres such as air and reducing atmospheres such as H2-rich gas mixtures) and maintain the temperature (e.g., 900°C) for fixed durations.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures in the range of about 800–1000°C; exposure atmospheres varying from air (oxidizing, ~0.21 atm O2) to reducing (pO2 near zero); exposure times on the order of several hours to enable observable oxidation and possible phase evolution.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and other defect-rich regions (characteristic of the additively manufactured microstructure) that act as fast diffusion pathways for Al and Ti, facilitating the preferential formation of oxide phases.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, the enhanced diffusion at grain boundaries leads to preferential oxidation of Al and Ti, forming non-protective or poorly adherent oxide scales that incite intergranular cracking. Conversely, in a reducing environment, disruption of the equilibrium between the protective oxides and the matrix may result in internal phase changes or coarsening that weaken the overall matrix integrity. In both cases, the local stress concentrations and the eventual loss of grain boundary cohesion trigger catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-built baseline, samples exposed in oxidizing atmospheres will display (a) a discontinuous or rapidly growing oxide scale concentrated along grain boundaries, (b) increased grain boundary embrittlement and crack initiation, and (c) notable reductions in ductility and ultimate strength. In reducing atmospheres, while surface oxidation may be suppressed, there will be evidence of internal microstructural destabilization (e.g., phase coarsening or non-protective phase formation) that also leads to loss of mechanical integrity.
generation.baseline: The as-built alloy exhibits a uniform FCC matrix with good mechanical properties (strength and ductility) and minimal pre-existing oxidation or grain boundary damage.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies for exposures in the temperature range 800–1000°C and atmospheres where oxygen partial pressure varies from that of air (~0.21 atm) to near-zero (reducing conditions). The exposure time should be sufficient (several hours) for diffusion-dominated oxidation or internal phase evolution to occur.
generation.uncertainty: The detailed kinetics of element-specific oxidation (particularly the roles of Ti vs. Al) and the interplay between oxidation and possible stress-induced phase transformations in reducing atmospheres are not fully characterized. The relative contribution of additive-induced defects versus intrinsic alloy behavior also remains to be quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy specimens and subject them to high-temperature (e.g., 900°C) exposure for a fixed duration under controlled atmospheres: one group in air (oxidizing) and another in a hydrogen-rich (reducing) environment. Post-exposure, characterize the samples using high-resolution microscopy (SEM/TEM) with EDS to assess oxide scale formation (thickness, continuity, and location), grain boundary integrity, and phase composition. Mechanical testing (tensile or bend tests) should then be performed to compare strength and ductility with the unexposed baseline.
measurements: Morphology and thickness of oxide layers at grain boundaries (via SEM/TEM and EDS)
Phase identification to detect formation of Al2O3, TiO2, or other non-protective phases (using XRD)
Mechanical property assessments (tensile strength, ductility, fracture mode analysis)
Fractography to correlate crack propagation with oxide location
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the oxidizing environment does not lead to preferential, discontinuous oxide formation at grain boundaries and no significant reduction in mechanical integrity (compared to the as-built state) is observed, the hypothesis that selective grain-boundary oxidation is the primary degradation mechanism will be falsified. Similarly, if reducing conditions yield the same degradation patterns or if degradation occurs independently of the controlling gas environment, the proposed mechanism would be rejected.

Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder

Abstract: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. The High Temperature Tensile and Creep Behaviors of High Entropy Superalloy

Abstract: AbstractThis article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L12 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThis work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe)2O4/Fe(Co,Cr)2O4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples.
